https://www.dw.com/en/nepal-floods-more-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JSU3 Extensive rescue operations are in full swing across the region Image: Skanda Gautam/ZUMA/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement The death toll from catastrophic flash floods along the border between Nepal and Tibet has risen to at least 165, while nearly 1,400 people were missing. Rescue teams were searching for survivors on Thursday, a day after a glacial collapse sent a huge wall of mud and rock barreling through the Himalayan communities, sweeping way entire villages. Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 826 people were missing in the country, almost 600 of them foreign nationals. In Tibet, Chinese broadcaster CCTV reported 558 people missing in Gyirong county, including 260 foreigners. Three deaths had been confirmed there as of Thursday morning, with two villagers rescued. Devastating flash floods hit northern Nepal To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What do we know about the flood in Nepal and Tibet? The disaster struck Wednesday when a glacial collapse triggered a flood in the Lhende Khola river, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi, in a corridor popular with trekkers and pilgrims connecting Kathmandu with Lhasa. Nepal police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle told Reuters the death toll was expected to keep climbing: "This will go up, as we have resumed the search and more bodies are expected to be recovered." Among those missing in Nepal were large numbers of foreign tourists. Sunil Sharma, a tourism board spokesperson, told the AP news agency that 133 of the missing were Indian pilgrims traveling to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a site sacred to Hindus, alongside 47 Americans, 34 Australians, 33 Britons and 24 Canadians. Reuters cited a slightly different breakdown from police and tourism officials, putting the missing tourists at 177 from India, 63 from the United States, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada. Many of the missing are foreigners visiting for treks or religious pilgrimages Image: Subaas Shrestha/NurPhoto/picture alliance More to come on this developing story... https://www.politico.eu/article/novo-tur.text: Novo and Anthropic announced a collaboration Wednesday to accelerate the development of new medicines and AI-driven software. The news landed hours after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke about the benefits of AI in health care — and days after tech bros warned there is a 10% likely existential threat to all humanity from super AI within the next decade. Anthopic also revealed last week scientists have tried to use Claude to develop bioweapons . Advertisement Advertisement That’s not deterring Novo, however. The Danish pharma giant said it would use the American artificial intelligence company’s models and Claude Science to advance its research as it aims to become “the world’s most AI-driven healthcare company.” "Joining forces with Anthropic will supercharge our R&D organisation and help us on our mission to bring new, transformative health solutions to people living with chronic diseases," Mike Doustdar, CEO of Novo, which has shortened its name from Novo Nordisk, said in a statement. “AI tools can also offer completely new scientific opportunities and aid reasoning and understanding of human biology and drug mechanics.” Anthropic CEO and co-founder Dario Amodei said using frontier AI models would shorten research timelines. “AI’s increasing capability brings with it the potential to compress a century’s worth of biological and medical breakthroughs into a decade,” he said. There will be “robust data governance and human oversight,” the statement added. Earlier today, von der Leyen used her State of the EU speech to say Europe needed to use AI in health , pointing to examples where it could be a game-changer like in the early detection of breast cancer through AI-supported mammography. Although she warned the technology needed to empower doctors, not replace them. Advertisement Advertisement
